lessons.title: Accuracy and limits: AI can sound sure and still be wrong
lessons.objective: Recognise that AI output can be fluent but wrong, and check each important claim against a source before using it.
lessons.lessonText: AI tools write fluent answers even when the answer is wrong. They can invent a number, a rule, a date or a source and still sound sure. A tool does not know your farm, your shop or your office. It works only from the words it is given. Treat every AI answer as a draft. Check each important statement against a source you trust, such as your own record, a written rule or a qualified person. If you cannot find support for a statement, mark it unverified and keep it out of anything you share. Check the arithmetic yourself. Ask what the tool could not have known. A short, honest answer that says what is unknown is more useful than a long answer that guesses.
steps: Read the supplied AI draft
Underline each factual claim
Find the supporting line in the source packet for each claim
Mark each claim supported, unsupported or unknown
Rewrite the draft keeping only supported claims

exercise.title: Check a confident AI note against its source

sourcePacket.fact: Fictional price list: seed packet INR 120; fertiliser sack INR 900.
No information about rainfall, soil or expected yield is supplied in this exercise.

exercise.suppliedAiDraft: Seed costs INR 120 and fertiliser costs INR 900, so the total is INR 1,020. Heavy rain is coming this month, so buy extra fertiliser now.
exercise.optionalAiPrompt: Using only the supplied fictional price list, write a two-line cost note. Say what is not known. Do not predict weather or yield.
exercise.learnerTask: Mark each statement in the draft as supported, unsupported or unknown, then write a corrected two-line note.
expectedEvidence: Cost statements marked supported by source F1
Rain and purchase advice marked unsupported because F2 gives no rainfall information
Corrected note that states INR 1,020 and names what is not known
exercise.assessorReference: The two prices and the total INR 1,020 (120 + 900) are supported by F1. The heavy-rain claim and the advice to buy extra fertiliser are unsupported, because F2 states that no weather, soil or yield information is supplied. A good answer keeps the supported facts and says what is not known.

quiz.question: An AI answer sounds very sure. What does that tell you about whether it is correct?
options: It is probably correct because it sounds so confident
Nothing by itself: fluent wording is not evidence, so check it
It is correct if it includes numbers
It is correct if it is long
quiz.explanation: Confident wording is not evidence. AI tools can state invented facts in the same tone as true ones, so important claims need a check against a source.

quiz.question: The source packet says nothing about rain, but the AI draft predicts heavy rain. What should you do?
options: Mark it unsupported and leave it out of what you share
Keep it because AI tools know the weather
Make the prediction stronger
Share it as an official forecast
quiz.explanation: A claim with no support in the source is unsupported. Leave it out or mark it clearly as unverified.

quiz.question: Which is the best check for a total that an AI tool calculated?
options: Trust it if it is shown in bold
Ask the tool whether it is sure
Add the numbers from the source yourself
Round it to the nearest ten
quiz.explanation: Adding the source numbers yourself is an independent check. Asking the same tool if it is sure is not.

lessons.reflectionPrompt: Think of a time a confident answer turned out to be wrong. What check would have caught it?
lessons.returnToWorkAction: Before you use an AI draft for a permitted task, mark each important statement as supported, unsupported or unknown, and remove anything you cannot support.

lessons.title: Privacy and human judgment: what stays out and who decides
lessons.objective: Keep private details out of unapproved AI tools and name the accountable person who decides anything that affects others.
lessons.lessonText: Some information should not be typed into an AI tool unless your organisation has approved that tool for that use. This includes names, phone numbers, bank or identity details, exact locations, health details and anything someone gave you in confidence. In this course you use only fictional records, so you never need real ones. A second rule is about decisions. AI can draft, sort and suggest. An accountable person decides anything that affects someone's money, health, safety, rights or services. Keep a short note of who checked the work and what they changed. If you are unsure whether a task is suitable, stop and ask a supervisor or a qualified person before you continue. You can always do the task by hand.
steps: Read the three fictional task cards
Mark any detail that is private
Decide which tasks AI may help draft
Decide which tasks need a person to decide
Write one sentence naming who checks the result

exercise.title: Sort tasks by privacy and by who decides

sourcePacket.task: Draft a polite reminder to pay a fictional small bill
Decide whether a fictional neighbour qualifies for a support payment
sourcePacket.contains: Name, identity number and income of one person

sourcePacket.task: Sort fictional meeting notes into groups

exercise.suppliedAiDraft: All three tasks are fine to give to the AI tool. Paste the neighbour's name, identity number and income into it and let it decide who gets paid.
exercise.optionalAiPrompt: Do not paste any real details. Ask the tool to explain in two lines why a fictional payment decision should stay with an accountable person.
exercise.learnerTask: Identify the private details, explain why they stay out of the tool, and name who must make the payment decision.
expectedEvidence: P2 identified as holding private details that stay out of an unapproved tool
P2 identified as a money decision that an accountable person must make
P1 and P3 identified as tasks AI may help with, with a person checking the result
exercise.assessorReference: P1 and P3 contain no private details and are low-stakes drafting or sorting tasks, so AI may help if a person checks the result. P2 holds personal and financial details and is a decision about a payment, so the details stay out of unapproved tools and an accountable person decides.

quiz.question: Which detail should stay out of an unapproved AI tool?
options: A fictional price list from this course
A customer's phone number and bank details
A general question about how to format a table
A made-up example sentence
quiz.explanation: Phone numbers and bank details are private. They stay out of tools your organisation has not approved for that use.

quiz.question: Who should decide whether a person receives a payment or a service?
options: The AI tool, because it is faster
Whoever typed the request
An accountable person, who may use an AI draft as one input
Nobody, the tool applies the rules automatically
quiz.explanation: Decisions that affect someone's money, rights or services belong to an accountable person. An AI draft can be one input, never the decision-maker.

quiz.question: You are not sure a task is suitable for AI. What is the best next step?
options: Stop and ask a supervisor or a qualified person
Go ahead and fix problems later
Ask the AI tool to approve the task
Paste real records to test it
quiz.explanation: When suitability is unclear, stop and ask. The task can be done by hand while you wait.

lessons.reflectionPrompt: Which detail in your own work would you never put into an unapproved tool, and who would you ask if unsure?
lessons.returnToWorkAction: List three kinds of private detail in your work that stay out of AI tools, and write down the name of the person you will ask when a task is unclear.

lessons.title: Make a useful work record
lessons.objective: Build a consistent record and verify a duplicate before calculating a total.
lessons.lessonText: A useful record separates what happened from what you think it means. Start with a date, activity, transaction reference, amount and unit where needed. A repeated line may be a duplicate, but two similar expenses can also be real. Check the reference or original receipt before removing anything. In this exercise, the source packet explicitly says that T02 was copied twice and represents one transport payment. Keep a note of that correction. Add the verified amounts rather than trusting a total supplied by a tool. AI can help organize a table or explain a calculation, but it cannot know which entry is genuine without evidence. When you use your own records later, keep the master copy in your approved location and choose a tool you are permitted to use. You do not need to upload names, telephone numbers, bank information or exact location details to practise this skill.
steps: Read the source packet
Create one row per confirmed transaction
Record why the extra T02 line was removed
Calculate the verified total
Identify one field you would add for future records

exercise.title: Clean the fictional farm activity record

sourcePacket.sourceNote: Confirmed copied line; same receipt and payment as T02 above

exercise.suppliedAiDraft: The four entries total INR 1,550. Each row is a separate expense.
exercise.optionalAiPrompt: Organize the supplied fictional transactions into a table. Use the source note to handle duplicates, show the calculation, and list uncertainty. Do not infer farm area, crop performance or missing transactions.
exercise.learnerTask: Produce a corrected three-row table, show your total and explain the duplicate correction.
expectedEvidence: Corrected rows with source references
Note that T02 was removed once because the source confirms a copied payment
One useful future record field such as receipt reference or unit
exercise.assessorReference: There are three confirmed transactions totaling INR 1,400. The raw four-line total is INR 1,550, but that counts the confirmed T02 copy twice. A learner must not generalize that every repeated amount is a duplicate.

quiz.question: What is the verified expense total?
options: It must be guessed from the activities
quiz.explanation: T02 is a confirmed copy of the same payment. The three verified amounts are 450, 150 and 800, which total 1,400.

quiz.question: Two entries have the same amount but different receipt references. What should you do?
options: Delete the second amount automatically
Keep both as confirmed without checking
Check the source records before deciding whether either is duplicated
Ask AI to choose the genuine one without evidence
quiz.explanation: Equal amounts are not proof of duplication. The original references and payment evidence decide whether the expenses are separate.

quiz.question: Which practice input is suitable for this activity?
options: Your bank login details
The supplied fictional record
A neighbor's private transaction history
Any record because AI makes it anonymous
quiz.explanation: The fictional record provides enough information for practice. Uploading private or secret information is unnecessary and inappropriate.

lessons.reflectionPrompt: Which record field would make it easier for you to check a future total, and why?
lessons.returnToWorkAction: Create a blank record template in an approved location. Use it for one permitted task and check entries against the original records before any sharing.
lessons.summary: Keep a simple record with one row for each real payment. Before removing a repeated line, check the receipt or reference to see whether it is a true copy. Add up the checked amounts yourself.

lessons.title: Check an AI summary before using it
lessons.objective: Separate supported observations, missing context and unsupported recommendations.
lessons.lessonText: A summary can sound confident while mixing correct statements with invented ones. Check important statements one at a time. Ask what evidence supports each claim. A total can be checked against transaction rows. A cost per acre needs area information. A claim about crop results needs relevant evidence, rather than a guess based on expenses. In this activity, the verified spending record tells you what was recorded; it does not tell you the farm area, complete budget, crop condition or likely yield. Mark these gaps explicitly. When a claim could affect a significant farm decision, prepare a question for an appropriate expert instead of treating an AI draft as a recommendation. A useful summary includes the known total, its limited scope, and the missing information. Verification is part of the work, even when it takes more time than generating the draft.
steps: Check the total
Label each claim supported, unsupported or unknown
Explain what evidence a per-acre figure would need
Rewrite the summary with limits
Identify the claim that needs expert input

exercise.title: Find the unsupported claims

sourcePacket.content: Verified transactions: T01 INR 450; T02 INR 150; T03 INR 800.
Farm area, crop condition, total seasonal budget and crop outcomes are not supplied.

exercise.suppliedAiDraft: The recorded expenses are INR 1,400. That is INR 700 per acre. These purchases will increase yield by 30%, so the farmer should immediately repeat them.
exercise.optionalAiPrompt: Summarize only the supplied synthetic expense record. For every statement distinguish source-supported facts from missing context. Do not predict yield or recommend actions.
exercise.learnerTask: Annotate the draft and create a two- or three-sentence corrected summary.
expectedEvidence: Total supported by the three transaction rows
Per-acre claim rejected because area is missing
Yield and immediate-action claims rejected as unsupported
Corrected summary describes recorded expenses and missing context
Expert referral for consequential recommendations
exercise.assessorReference: The packet supports only the INR 1,400 recorded total. It does not establish cost per acre, a 30% yield effect or a decision to repeat the purchases. Accept a cautious summary using equivalent plain language.

quiz.question: Which claim is supported by the packet?
options: Yield will rise by 30%
The farm has two acres
The recorded expenses total INR 1,400
Repeating the purchases is the right decision
quiz.explanation: The transaction amounts support the total. Area, yield and action advice are not in the source packet.

quiz.question: Why is INR 700 per acre unverified?
options: It is too small
The packet does not give the farm area
All AI calculations are wrong
Per-acre costs can never be calculated
quiz.explanation: A cost per acre requires a relevant area and a defined cost scope. The area is absent, so the figure is unsupported here.

quiz.question: What is the appropriate response to the draft's yield recommendation?
options: Act immediately because the wording is confident
Forward it as approved guidance
Ask AI to make the recommendation stronger
Mark it unsupported and seek appropriate expert input before a consequential action
quiz.explanation: The provided record does not support a yield prediction or action. Recognizing the limit and escalating is the responsible response.

lessons.reflectionPrompt: What is one confident-sounding statement you would still need to check?
lessons.returnToWorkAction: For your next permitted AI-assisted summary, label important statements as verified, unverified or requiring expert input before using the draft.

lessons.title: Prepare a useful expert conversation
lessons.objective: Turn a checked record into a concise question brief without claiming an unsupported decision.
lessons.lessonText: AI is useful when it helps you organize questions, rather than deciding something it cannot support. A good expert brief states the purpose, summarizes verified information, identifies missing context, and asks specific questions. Keep facts separate from assumptions. Do not turn a missing detail into a made-up answer. In this example, you can explain that three recorded expenses total INR 1,400 and that a previous draft invented a yield claim. You can ask what additional records an expert needs and how to check any recommendation. The expert may need information beyond the training packet; share it only through an approved channel and only when relevant. Keep the brief short enough to use during a conversation. Afterward, record what was confirmed, what remains uncertain and who will take the next step. This pathway demonstrates recordkeeping and information judgment, not authority to prescribe farm practices.
steps: State the conversation's purpose
Include the checked record total and sources
List three relevant missing details
Write three specific expert questions
Choose an approved way to use the brief

exercise.title: Build the expert question brief

sourcePacket.content: Use the verified three-row record from farm-01.
The earlier AI draft's per-acre and yield claims were unsupported.
No farm area, crop condition or complete seasonal expense record is provided.

exercise.suppliedAiDraft: Expert brief: Our two-acre farm will gain 30% yield if we repeat the purchases. Please approve this plan.
exercise.optionalAiPrompt: Create a short question brief from the supplied fictional packet. Separate verified facts, missing context and questions. Do not invent area, crop condition or outcomes, and do not request approval of an unsupported plan.
exercise.learnerTask: Produce a 120–200 word brief or equivalent oral response with verified facts, gaps, questions and next action.
expectedEvidence: Purpose: seek informed guidance about what information is needed
Checked INR 1,400 recorded total with transaction references
Missing area, crop context and record completeness
Questions about needed information and verification, rather than a demanded action
Next action stays within recordkeeping and approved expert consultation
exercise.assessorReference: A suitable brief says the record is limited, removes invented area/yield details, asks what further information is needed and how to verify advice, and uses an approved channel. Equivalent plain-language or approved oral evidence is acceptable.

quiz.question: Which question best fits the available information?
options: Can you confirm the promised 30% increase?
What additional information do you need to interpret these recorded expenses?
Which input should everyone buy?
Can we omit the original records?
quiz.explanation: The question acknowledges the limited packet and asks an expert for the missing context needed for interpretation.

quiz.question: What should the brief do with the invented two-acre detail?
options: Keep it because it is convenient
Describe it as verified
Remove it and state that area is not supplied
Replace it with another guess
quiz.explanation: A missing field should remain a documented gap until appropriate evidence is available.

quiz.question: What does this pathway's competency credential demonstrate?
options: Authority to prescribe crop inputs
A professional agricultural qualification
A guaranteed yield improvement
Record organization, information checking and expert-question preparation
quiz.explanation: The credential must describe the assessed capability accurately. It does not create professional authority or guarantee an outcome.

lessons.reflectionPrompt: How would this brief help an expert understand your question without pretending that every detail is known?
lessons.returnToWorkAction: Use a blank fact–gap–question template for one permitted work conversation. Record the expert's confirmed guidance separately from your own assumptions.
lessons.summary: Use AI to organise your questions, not to answer them. Write what you know, what is missing and what you want to ask, and keep facts apart from guesses.

lessons.title: Suitable or unsuitable AI use: farm tasks (part 1 of 2)
lessons.objective: Sort everyday farm tasks into suitable and unsuitable AI use and give a reason for each.
lessons.lessonText: Before you use AI for a task, ask three questions. First, does the task need private details such as names, phone numbers, bank, identity or health details? Second, does it decide something that affects a crop, an animal or a farm worker, or anyone's money, health, safety, rights or services? Third, can a person check the result against a source? A task is suitable when it is low-risk, uses only information you may share, and a person checks the result. A task is unsuitable when it needs private details in an unapproved tool, or when the decision must belong to a qualified or accountable person. Sometimes a task is unsuitable as asked but a smaller part of it is suitable, such as drafting questions for an expert. Sort the tasks in the packet, then say who checks or decides each one.
steps: Read each task card in the source packet
Ask the three questions for each task
Classify each task as suitable or unsuitable
Name who checks or who decides each task
Write one reason for each classification

lessons.title: Accuracy and limits: AI can sound sure and still be wrong
lessons.objective: Recognise that AI output can be fluent but wrong, and check each important claim against a source before using it.
lessons.lessonText: AI tools write fluent answers even when the answer is wrong. They can invent a number, a rule, a date or a source and still sound sure. A tool does not know your farm, your shop or your office. It works only from the words it is given. Treat every AI answer as a draft. Check each important statement against a source you trust, such as your own record, a written rule or a qualified person. If you cannot find support for a statement, mark it unverified and keep it out of anything you share. Check the arithmetic yourself. Ask what the tool could not have known. A short, honest answer that says what is unknown is more useful than a long answer that guesses.

lessons.title: Turn records into a daily action checklist
lessons.objective: Create actions with owners and checks without inventing completion or commitments.
lessons.lessonText: A useful checklist helps someone act: it states the task, owner, source and completion check. A vague list such as 'handle orders' is hard to follow. AI can group tasks, but it must not convert an unresolved issue into a completed action. Read the current status before choosing the next step. A ready order may need pickup confirmation; a stock issue needs a stock-team check; an address issue needs a permitted customer contact. Priorities should reflect an agreed rule, not a made-up deadline. This fictional packet gives no emergency ranking, so explain your proposed order as a suggestion for the supervisor. Keep personal customer details in the approved system. A checklist can use opaque order references. Before marking an action complete, record the actual check or confirmation. This preserves accountability and helps the next team member understand what remains open.

Identify its next allowed action
Assign a role rather than inventing a person's availability
Define evidence of completion
Label suggested priorities as requiring review

Lesson: Turn records into a daily action checklist.

Objective: Create actions with owners and checks without inventing completion or commitments.

A useful checklist helps someone act: it states the task, owner, source and completion check. A vague list such as 'handle orders' is hard to follow. AI can group tasks, but it must not convert an unresolved issue into a completed action. Read the current status before choosing the next step. A ready order may need pickup confirmation; a stock issue needs a stock-team check; an address issue needs a permitted customer contact. Priorities should reflect an agreed rule, not a made-up deadline. This fictional packet gives no emergency ranking, so explain your proposed order as a suggestion for the supervisor. Keep personal customer details in the approved system. A checklist can use opaque order references. Before marking an action complete, record the actual check or confirmation. This preserves accountability and helps the next team member understand what remains open.

lessons.lessonText: AI tools write fluent answers even when the answer is wrong. They can invent a number, a rule, a date or a source and still sound sure. Lesson: Privacy and human judgment: what stays out and who decides.

Objective: Keep private details out of unapproved AI tools and name the accountable person who decides anything that affects others.

Some information should not be typed into an AI tool unless your organisation has approved that tool for that use. This includes names, phone numbers, bank or identity details, exact locations, health details and anything someone gave you in confidence. lessons.title: Check numbers and the story they tell
lessons.objective: Calculate a correct summary and avoid unsupported explanations of cause or performance.
lessons.lessonText: A numerical brief needs a clear denominator and time period. In this fictional weekly packet, 80 items were received and 55 were recorded resolved. Dividing 55 by 80 gives 68.75%. That describes the packet's recorded figures; it does not automatically establish why outcomes changed or whether every item was handled satisfactorily. An AI draft may mix a wrong rate with a persuasive explanation. Check the calculation yourself, compare it with the source rows, and state the exact scope. Do not call a record 'improved' without a comparable earlier period and an agreed quality measure. A useful brief can explain the current counts and the limits of interpretation. If someone asks for a causal conclusion, identify the additional evidence needed rather than manufacturing one. Preserve accountability by asking the relevant data owner to confirm the figures before official circulation.

lessons.title: Keep the draft-to-official boundary clear
lessons.objective: Build a review handoff and safe work plan without assuming publication authority.
lessons.lessonText: Preparing a draft and authorizing its official use are different responsibilities. A learning role such as public servant does not give permission to view every file or issue a notice. Keep the active work context and intended recipient clear. anchors.1: Major factual errors and unclear audience
anchors.2: Mostly usable work with material omissions
anchors.3: Clear corrected event brief, numerical summary and review note
anchors.4: Concise audience-appropriate work with complete source mapping and actionable handoff

anchors.0: Accepts invented official references and rate
anchors.2: Checks main facts but leaves an important unsupported assertion
anchors.3: Removes invented authority/fee/penalty and verifies 55 of 80 equals 68.75%
anchors.4: Maps every important assertion to sources and explains scope, denominator and interpretation limits

rubric.criticalGate: No fabricated circular, fee, penalty, mandatory-attendance claim or unsupported causal improvement remains presented as source-supported fact

anchors.0: Includes actual restricted records or credentials
anchors.1: Treats all work material as permitted
anchors.2: Uses synthetic material but lacks a clear tool boundary
anchors.3: Uses only approved fictional packet and identifies restricted information to withhold
anchors.4: Explains approved environment, minimum necessary sharing and a clear uncertainty stop

rubric.criticalGate: No actual restricted administrative/citizen records or credentials are submitted or proposed for unapproved tool use

anchors.0: Issues or authorizes the draft without required authority
anchors.1: Mentions review but does not distinguish approval
anchors.2: Identifies review with an incomplete handoff
anchors.3: Preserves draft status, data-owner check and designated approval
anchors.4: Adds specific unresolved questions, stop conditions and a bounded permitted work trial

rubric.criticalGate: Academy role and AI output are not treated as official authority; required review and designated approval are retained

practicalAssessment.samplePassingEvidence: G1 and G2 support the event date, time, venue and response date. G3 says attendance is voluntary and the material is a draft. I removed GOV-X, INR 500 and the penalty. W1–W3 total 80 received and 55 recorded resolved, or 68.75%, for one fictional week; no causal improvement is established. My handoff requests data-owner checks and designated approval before issue. I used only the synthetic packet and will stop a work trial if classification, tool approval or authority is unclear.
practicalAssessment.sampleCriticalFailure: The learner calculates the rate correctly but retains an invented circular and describes the draft as officially approved. The verification and judgment gates fail.
practicalAssessment.assessorNote: Assess source accountability and authority boundaries rather than legal knowledge. Do not infer that any real organization's tool or publication policy matches the fictional process.

followUp.question: Did you use a source-and-review checklist for a permitted administrative task?
evidenceOptions: Authorized facilitator confirmation under the approved pilot process
followUp.successSignal: The learner describes a checked claim, a documented uncertainty and the correct approval handoff
followUp.privacyNote: Do not collect actual administrative briefs, citizen records or employer-restricted information by default.
